judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: The article's featured image (Sem-Titulo-4.jpg) is a generic stock photo of a doctor listening to an older woman patient, with alt="". It holds no text or data and adds nothing the title and article do not already say, so a null alt for an ambient illustration meets 1.1.1 (WAI decorative-images guidance). Some auditors would like a short alt on featured photos, but that is advice, not a failure. The live HTML has the same img with alt="", and the screenshot shows the same photo.

judgments.label: uncertain
judgments.rationale: This is the icon-only Twitter share link in the bottom 'Compartilhe' bar: a white Twitter bird on a #55acee circle. Screenshot pixels confirm #ffffff on #55acee (2.46:1), and the circle against the white page is also 2.46:1, so the measurement and the sentence are right. But the glyph is the Twitter brand logo in Twitter's former brand blue. Understanding 1.4.11 exempts logos under the essential exception and says that exemption normatively carries over to a UI component whose only content is the logo; a contrasting variant is only encouraged. Auditors split on applying this to plugin share icons. I lean to a pass, so the label is uncertain. The live HTML has the same inline colours.

judgments.label: true_positive
judgments.rationale: A Novartis logo image (alt="") sits in its own paragraph after the article's last paragraph, before the comment prompt. The word Novartis appears nowhere in the page text (I searched the whole snapshot). So the logo, which signals that the company is linked to the content (most likely as a supporter), carries information a screen reader user loses. A logo is informative and needs its name as the alternative; no decorative reading holds up. The live HTML still has alt="". The claim names this failure.

judgments.label: false_positive

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: This is the seek slider of the GSpeech audio player (role=slider, aria-label 'Audio position'). 2.4.6 asks that labels describe topic or purpose. 'Audio position' says what the slider sets (the playback position), and a slider takes no typed entry, so 'does not say what to enter' is neither true nor the criterion's test. An English label on a pt-BR page is a 3.1.2 matter, not 2.4.6. The player is injected by script and is not in the static HTML I fetched, so I could not compare it with the live page.

judgments.label: true_positive
judgments.rationale: This is the sidebar newsletter sign-up field (input type=email name=ne, aria-label 'E-mail'). It collects the visitor's own email address, which is a listed input purpose ('email'). It has no autocomplete attribute, either in the snapshot or in the live HTML. type=email only states the data format, not that the value is the user's own address, and it is not a sufficient technique (H98 is). I found no reason the field would be exempt. The claim names the failure.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: This is the pie chart image 'Onde realiza o tratamento', with alt="". The paragraph just before it, in the same section, states every value: 48,2% SUS only, 37,3% health plan, 9,6% both, and almost 5% paying out of pocket. So the claim that the image conveys something the text does not say is false of the capture. A null alt on an image fully repeated by adjacent text is acceptable (WAI's 'image with adjacent text alternative'). That paragraph was in the element's context, so the model judged wrongly. The live HTML is identical.

It does drop the full name, tagline and URL, though the paragraph right after it gives the full name. A logo usually takes its organisation's name as the alt, so I lean to a pass; other auditors would fail an alt that copies a section title instead of describing the image. Hence uncertain.
